title: The Tragedy of Having a Wikipedia Page—and Then Losing It
gist: Wired's long feature on Wikipedia deletions follows people whose biographies were nominated for deletion for lack of notability, centering on a bitter editor dispute over analog astronaut Martina Dimoska's page. It argues a Wikipedia page gives real professional credibility, while volunteer editors apply a verifiability standard that can feel arbitrary.

insights.claim: Dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies are purged every day for not meeting notability thresholds, because volunteers are limited even though the English site hosts more than 7 million articles and has no space constraint.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Moderation capacity, not storage, is what limits the encyclopedia, which rations attention.
insights.locator: All three have had a biography

insights.claim: Wikipedia's operating test is verifiability, not truth: an unproven claim about a Civil War officer drinking mustard in battle sat in his biography for 17 years and was removed for lack of reliable evidence, not because it was disproven.
insights.speaker: Britta Gustafson
insights.so_what: Sourcing norms make Wikipedia a lagging reflection of secondary-source coverage.
insights.quote: “We’re not really looking for what’s true,”

insights.claim: Deletion debates can be decided simply because nobody shows up, as participation is voluntary, so outcomes depend heavily on which editors engage.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Outcomes are partly random, driven by volunteer attention.
insights.quote: Articles, once marked for death, can be deleted simply because nobody showed up to debate the matter.
insights.locator: There is, when you look for it

insights.claim: Editors noted that a person's request to delete their own page is not grounds for deletion, though it can tip a no-consensus decision, and that subjects cannot edit their own biographies without disclosing a conflict of interest.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: The subject of the article has little control over their page.

insights.claim: Subjects see a page as a credential: an orthopedist says it helps him get hired as an expert witness, and a French-Iranian adviser says it inspires confidence, and she suspects it made the media pick her as a commentator.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: A Wikipedia biography functions as a trust signal in professional markets and creates a self-reinforcing loop of coverage.

insights.claim: There is a chicken-and-egg loop in which more media coverage proves notability and a Wikipedia page encourages more coverage.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Early recognition compounds and exclusion is hard to reverse.

insights.claim: Wikipedia editor Britta Gustafson admits that having an article 'says something' and 'implies something', even though editors say coverage is not a prize.
insights.speaker: Britta Gustafson
insights.so_what: Editors' self-image as neutral gatekeepers conflicts with how the outside world treats a page.

insights.claim: Borderline-notable subjects are at risk, and an editor warned it is folly to celebrate becoming the subject of an article, as Dimoska's public celebration was followed by a deletion nomination the next day.
insights.speaker: Anne Clin
insights.so_what: Promoting a page can attract the scrutiny that gets it deleted.
insights.locator: Anne Clin, who has edited Wikipedia

insights.claim: Even Wikipedia insiders want pages: Kiril Simeonovski created a page about himself soon after joining in 2008, which was promptly deleted, and Jimmy Wales has been caught editing his own biography.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Desire for validation affects even those who enforce the rules.
insights.locator: Wikipedia pages, for better or worse

insights.claim: Simeonovski nominated Dimoska's page for deletion as promotional, with weak sourcing including LinkedIn posts, and was suspicious that she posted celebrating it right after approval; the closing editor ruled no consensus, citing bludgeoning, canvassing and sockpuppetry.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Procedural messiness and sockpuppet behavior can decide a case more than the merits.
insights.quote: Given the bludgeoning, canvassing, and sockpuppetry evident here

insights.claim: Dimoska denies editing the page and the page stayed with a 'promotional content' disclaimer; she knew Simeonovski through mutual friends and said small-community recognition can draw more scrutiny than expected.
insights.speaker: Martina Dimoska
insights.so_what: Social-media proximity in a small community can shape deletion disputes.

insights.claim: A closing editor said the arguments to delete were stronger on the merits but sufficient reasoned opposition existed, so persistence outweighed the merits.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Obstinacy can beat the stronger argument in consensus systems.

insights.claim: A user claimed that surgeon Sheldon Marks wanted his page removed, but Marks later said the statements were fabrications and he wanted to keep it; editors had already voted to delete.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Impersonation can be used in deletion requests, and editors do not tightly verify who is speaking.

insights.claim: Several deleted pages came from sources like a 17-year-old page created by an admirer for an artist who is now a psychotherapist, or a singer deleted and redirected to her one famous song, showing the standard treats single-credit careers as non-notable.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Notability is judged on lifetime coverage, so outdated pages often fall away.

insights.claim: Veteran editors' verdicts can be dismissive in tone, for example 'This guy is a nobody. Delete him.', and subjects who find out about their deletions typically learn it from the reporter.
insights.speaker: Duncan Fyfe
insights.so_what: Casual, abrasive tone adds reputational damage for people who see their page as a credential.
insights.quote: “This guy is a nobody. Delete him.”
insights.locator: There is, when you look for it
